messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 57

Ana arrived at her fourth session already apologizing, her handbag clutched against her chest like a shield. She is a 37-year-old Latin American woman, a hotel manager, and she has been living with her partner, Marco, for three years. She speaks in a careful, precise way, as if she is still composing emails to guests and staff, but her hands never stop moving—folding the edge of her sleeve, pressing her thumbnail into her palm.

The assault happened eighteen months ago, at the annual hospitality industry gala. Ana remembers the sequins on her dress, the way they caught the light. She remembers the champagne flute in her hand, the warmth of the ballroom, the noise. She remembers a regional director she had known for years, a man with a kind smile and a firm handshake. He offered to walk her to her car. She said yes.

She remembers the parking garage. The echo of her heels. The sudden shift in his voice, low and close to her ear. She remembers the concrete pillar pressing into her back, the smell of his cologne, the way her body went still—a manager’s composure, she tells herself now, a survival instinct she didn’t know she had. She did not scream. She did not fight. She stood frozen, calculating exits that weren’t there, until it was over.

She drove home. She showered. She did not tell Marco. She did not tell anyone.

The next morning, she went to work. She greeted the front desk staff. She reviewed the weekend bookings. She approved a new linen vendor. She did not cry. She tells me this with a faint, hollow smile, as if it is a point of pride. “I handled it,” she says. “I always handle things.”

But she has not handled it. The hypervigilance began within weeks. She cannot walk through the hotel lobby without scanning every face, every doorway. She has changed the staff schedule so she never works late. She avoids the parking garage entirely, taking the bus instead, even though it adds forty minutes to her commute. She has stopped attending any industry events, claiming scheduling conflicts. Her regional director still emails her. She deletes them without reading, her heart pounding, her palms slick.

Marco has noticed. He asks if she is okay. She says she is tired. She says work is demanding. She pulls away when he touches her waist, when he comes up behind her in the kitchen. She cannot explain why. The memory of that concrete pillar is too close. She feels his hands on her body and thinks of the other hands, the ones that did not ask. She has started sleeping on the far edge of the bed, her back to him, her legs tense.

The nightmares began four months ago. She does not see the man’s face. She sees the garage, the fluorescent lights, the oil stains on the concrete. She wakes gasping, her nightgown soaked, her heart a trapped bird. She does not wake Marco. She lies still and listens to the silence, her mind cataloging every sound—the creak of the house, the hum of the refrigerator, the possibility of footsteps.

At work, she is still competent, still praised. But her staff has noticed she startles easily. A dropped tray in the kitchen makes her flinch. A guest tapping her shoulder makes her spin around, breathless, her smile a mask that slips for just a second before she recovers. She has started drinking a glass of wine at night to sleep, then two. She tells herself it is not a problem. She tells herself she is fine.

She is not fine. She is exhausted. She is afraid. She is ashamed of her own silence, of the way she stood still in that garage, of the fact that she still says “fine” when Marco asks. She is here, in this room, because a housekeeper found her crying in the laundry room three weeks ago, and that housekeeper—a woman named Elena who fled her own country—sat down beside her and said, “You do not have to carry this alone.”

Ana is trying to believe her.
